Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Texas transfer on death deed (TOD deed) lets an owner name a beneficiary who receives the real estate at the owner's death, without probate for that property. The law is Estates Code Chapter 114, and a deed only works if it is recorded with the county clerk before the owner dies. This guide covers what the statute requires, what the beneficiary receives and how to sell the house afterward.

What is a transfer on death deed in Texas?

A transfer on death deed is a deed that takes effect when the owner dies. Chapter 114 allows an individual to transfer an interest in real property to one or more beneficiaries this way (Sec. 114.051), and the chapter may be cited as the Texas Real Property Transfer on Death Act (Sec. 114.001). It applies to deeds signed and acknowledged on or after September 1, 2015, by an owner who died on or after that date (Sec. 114.003).

The deed stays revocable no matter what it says (Sec. 114.052). During the owner's life it does not give the beneficiary any interest, and it does not stop the owner from selling or borrowing against the house (Sec. 114.101). It also does not trigger a due-on-sale clause or affect the homestead exemption or the age 65 and disability exemptions.

What does a valid TOD deed need?

Sec. 114.055 sets three requirements. The deed must contain the essential elements and formalities of a recordable deed. It must state that the transfer to the beneficiary happens at the owner's death. And it must be recorded before the owner's death in the deed records of the county clerk's office in the county where the property sits.

The owner needs the same capacity required to make a contract (Sec. 114.054). A TOD deed cannot be created through a power of attorney, so an agent cannot sign one for the owner. The beneficiary does not have to be told, receive the deed or accept it while the owner is alive, and no payment is required (Sec. 114.056).

If the deed is never recorded before death, it does not work, and the house goes through the owner's will or Texas intestacy rules instead.

How is a TOD deed changed or revoked?

An owner can revoke by recording a later TOD deed or an express revocation that is acknowledged after the deed it revokes and recorded in the same county before death (Sec. 114.057). A will cannot revoke or override a TOD deed. When joint owners with a right of survivorship made the deed, it is revoked only if all living owners revoke it.

An owner who sells the house after signing a TOD deed can defeat it too. A later conveyance is valid against the beneficiary if a deed or memorandum of that sale is recorded in the same county before the owner's death (Sec. 114.102).

What does the beneficiary receive?

The beneficiary must outlive the owner by 120 hours. If not, that share lapses and passes as if the deed were a gift in a will (Sec. 114.103). Several beneficiaries take equal undivided shares with no right of survivorship unless the deed says otherwise. The property passes without any warranty of title, even if the deed claims one.

The beneficiary takes the house subject to any mortgage, lien or other encumbrance on it at the owner's death (Sec. 114.104). If the rest of the estate cannot cover debts, expenses, estate tax and certain family allowances, a personal representative can reach TOD-deed property, and a proceeding must start within two years of the death (Sec. 114.106). A beneficiary can also disclaim the interest under Chapter 122 (Sec. 114.105).

Recording the deed after the owner dies

The TOD deed itself is already recorded in the county deed records. To sell, a buyer and the title company will usually want proof that the owner died and that the beneficiary survived. The statute does not list those papers, so ask the title company what it requires before you list. We did not find an official page on those closing documents, so we do not state a list here.

Texas transfer on death deed FAQ

Is a transfer on death deed legal in Texas?

Yes. Estates Code Chapter 114 authorizes it for deeds signed and acknowledged on or after September 1, 2015 (Secs. 114.051 and 114.003).

When must a Texas TOD deed be recorded?

Before the owner's death, in the deed records of the county clerk's office where the property is located (Sec. 114.055).

Can a TOD deed avoid probate in Texas?

The property passes to the beneficiary at death without a probate transfer of that house. The beneficiary still takes it subject to mortgages and liens, and a personal representative can reach it for estate debts within two years of the death in some cases (Secs. 114.104 and 114.106).

Can the owner sell the house after signing a TOD deed?

Yes. The deed does not limit the owner's right to sell or mortgage the property during life (Sec. 114.101).

content:
Lady Bird Deed in Texas: What the Law Says and What to Do

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Lady Bird Deed in Texas: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Lady Bird Deed in Texas sale
  • Turn the Lady Bird Deed in Texas offer down and you owe us nothing

Own a House Through a Lady Bird Deed? Get a Cash Offer

If you hold or inherited a house conveyed by an enhanced life estate or lady bird deed, we can look at it as-is. Tell us about the property.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas statutes do not use the term "lady bird deed." We searched the full text of Property Code Chapter 5 and Estates Code Chapter 114 and found neither "lady bird" nor "enhanced life estate." People still use the name for a deed that keeps a life estate for the owner with powers to sell, so this guide explains what Texas statutes say about the pieces involved and where we cannot confirm anything from an official source.

What people mean by a lady bird deed

A lady bird deed, also called an enhanced life estate deed, is a name used for a deed in which an owner keeps a life estate and the power to sell or mortgage, and names someone to take the property at death. That description comes from common usage, and Texas statutes do not define it. We found no official Texas page that explains the instrument, so we do not state how courts or agencies treat it.

What Texas statutes do say

  • An owner may make a conveyance during life of an estate that begins in the future, in the same way as by will (Sec. 5.041).
  • A life tenant given the power to sell and reinvest life estate property owes the duties of a trustee for that sale. A life tenant who simply keeps the property still owes common-law life tenant duties (Sec. 5.009).

Together these show that a life estate and a future interest can be created by deed. They do not tell you how a particular lady bird deed will be read.

Holding an enhanced life estate deed?
Tell us about the property. We can review it as-is and explain how a sale would close.
Get My Cash Offer →

How it differs from a TOD deed

Estates Code Sec. 114.002 defines a transfer on death deed as a deed authorized by Chapter 114 and says the term does not refer to any other deed that transfers an interest on death. That means a lady bird deed is a different instrument from a statutory Texas transfer on death deed. The TOD statute is also nonexclusive and does not limit other lawful ways to transfer real property (Sec. 114.004).

What we could not confirm

  • How Texas courts treat lady bird deeds, including creditor claims and the owner's retained powers.
  • Medicaid estate recovery, property tax and capital gains effects. The sources we found were law firm, library and case-reporter sites, which are outside the official sources we rely on.
  • Whether other Texas statutes outside Chapter 5 and Chapter 114 mention the term.

If you hold or are inheriting under one of these deeds, a Texas real estate attorney can read the specific document. The wording of the deed decides what rights exist.

Lady bird deed Texas FAQ

Is a lady bird deed recognized in Texas?

Texas statutes do not use the term. Property Code Chapter 5 and Estates Code Chapter 114 contain neither 'lady bird' nor 'enhanced life estate,' so a lawyer needs to read the specific deed.

Is a lady bird deed the same as a transfer on death deed?

No. Estates Code Sec. 114.002 says a transfer on death deed means a deed authorized by Chapter 114 and does not refer to any other deed that transfers an interest at death.

Does a deed have to be recorded?

A deed must be signed and acknowledged or sworn to be recorded with the county clerk (Property Code Sec. 12.001). Whether recording is required for a particular deed to work depends on its type and wording, so ask an attorney.

Can I sell a house held under a life estate deed?

Often yes, but who must sign depends on the deed. Title companies read the recorded deed to decide.

What is a lady bird deed in Texas?

A lady bird deed is the popular name for an enhanced life estate deed, a deed that names who inherits a house while the owner keeps full ownership and control during life. The Texas State Law Library says the owner can live on the property, sell it, and change or revoke the deed at any time. It describes the instrument as governed by common law, which means no Texas statute spells out its form.

The library adds that no official form exists. Sample language appears in legal publications, and it recommends talking to a lawyer before signing, since a drafting mistake can have serious consequences. Because the deed names the person who takes the house at death, it can move real property outside probate, the same goal a will serves through the court.

A seller who holds a house this way usually faces a different set of questions than an owner with a plain warranty deed. Who has to sign, what the lender thinks, and what the county clerk needs on file all depend on the wording of the recorded deed.

How is a lady bird deed different from a transfer on death deed or a life estate?

The State Law Library compares the three instruments side by side, and the gaps matter most when a sale is on the table. A statutory transfer on death deed (TODD) falls under Chapter 114 of the Estates Code, the Texas Real Property Transfer on Death Act. A lady bird deed does not.

Lady bird deed and transfer on death deed compared, from the Texas State Law Library
FeatureLady bird deedTransfer on death deed
Legal basisCommon lawEstates Code Chapter 114
Backup beneficiariesNot allowedAllowed
Mortgage due-on-sale clauseMay sometimes be triggered at the owner's deathNot triggered (Sec. 114.101(5))
Signed under a power of attorneyPossible if the power of attorney authorizes itNot possible (Sec. 114.054)
Warranty of titleGeneral, special or noneNone allowed (Sec. 114.103(d))
Selling and creditor claimsMay be hard to sell without the beneficiary's approvalProperty stays open to estate creditor claims for two years after death (Sec. 114.106)

A standard life estate deed is a different animal. The beneficiary gets an interest right away, so the owner generally cannot sell or mortgage without that person's consent, sale proceeds are shared, and the beneficiary's creditors or a divorce court can reach the interest. Those deeds are mostly permanent, while the enhanced version can generally be changed or revoked.

Can I sell a house held under a lady bird deed?

Yes, the State Law Library says the owner keeps full ownership and control and may sell. Its comparison table does warn that a sale can be hard to complete without the beneficiary's approval, so a buyer's closing agent will read the recorded deed first. Have a certified copy ready and expect questions about whether the beneficiary needs to sign.

  • Lender issues. A mortgage on the property may carry a due-on-sale clause that a lady bird deed can trigger at death, so ask the servicer about the loan before relying on the deed.
  • Signature authority. If an agent under a power of attorney signed the deed, the power of attorney itself must have authorized that kind of transfer.
  • Warranty language. A deed can be drafted with a general warranty, a special warranty or no warranty, and the closing agent will see which one applies.
  • Recording. The deed has to be signed and acknowledged to be recorded, and it is filed with the county clerk of the county where the property sits (Property Code 12.001(b)).

If you changed your mind about who inherits, the library says an enhanced life estate deed can generally be revoked. Do that with a recorded document prepared by a lawyer, not by informal notes.

Does a lady bird deed protect a Texas home from Medicaid estate recovery?

It may sometimes, according to the State Law Library, which notes that lady bird deeds are occasionally used to shield real property from Medicaid estate recovery claims. Whether it works in a particular case is a question for an elder law attorney.

Texas Health and Human Services explains that its Medicaid Estate Recovery Program (MERP) reaches only long-term care services received after age 55 and only for people who began receiving them after March 1, 2005. Nursing facility care and several waiver programs are covered, such as STAR+PLUS long-term care services and Community Attendant Services. The state never asks for more than it paid, and it takes debts such as funeral costs and a mortgage into account before a claim is paid.

  • No claim is made while a spouse is alive, or when there is a child under 21 or a child who is blind or permanently disabled.
  • No claim is made when the estate is worth $15,000 or less or the Medicaid costs are $5,000 or less.
  • An unmarried adult child who lived in the home full time for at least a year before the death can also stop a claim.
  • Heirs may ask for an undue hardship waiver and must provide proof.

For a specific case, the agency's contractor can be reached at 800-641-9356. The agency also says it looks back up to 60 months at asset transfers made before applying for nursing home or waiver services, so timing a deed can matter.

What happens to the house after the owner of a lady bird deed dies?

The beneficiary named in the deed takes the house without a probate case, but the county records still have to show it. Practice form books list an affidavit of death used to transfer title under a transfer on death or lady bird deed, and the State Law Library says a TODD needs an affidavit of death and a death certificate recorded with the clerk where the property is located. Ask the clerk or a title company which documents they expect for the deed in your file.

When no such deed exists, other paths apply. A will can be probated within four years of death, a muniment of title lets a will prove ownership when the only debts are real estate liens, and a small estate affidavit works for estates of $75,000 or less excluding homestead and exempt property. Texas repealed its inheritance tax effective September 1, 2015.

On the tax side, a beneficiary who moves into the inherited house applies for a homestead exemption with the appraisal district. An heir not named on a recorded deed gives the district an affidavit of ownership interest, the owner's death certificate and a recent utility bill. Schools must grant $140,000 off the value of a residence homestead, and age 65 or older or disabled owners get an additional $60,000.

Where can I get help with a lady bird deed in Texas?

Start with a lawyer who handles estate planning, since the State Law Library will not tell anyone what the law means for their situation. Its Legal Help page lists ways to find one. Law libraries also keep practice forms, among them a lady bird deed form in Texas Estate Planning and another in Davis's Texas Estate Planning Forms.

The Tarrant County law library's research guide points to Texas Administrative Code Title 1, Section 358.350 on life estates and remainder interests, along with Property Code 5.009 on the duties of a life tenant. Both are worth showing to the attorney who drafts or reviews your deed.

If you inherited a house through one of these deeds and want to sell it, send us the recorded deed and the basic facts. We buy houses as-is, and the closing agent will confirm which documents the county clerk needs before the sale.

More questions about Lady Bird Deed in Texas

Is a lady bird deed legal in Texas?

The State Law Library describes it as an enhanced life estate deed governed by common law. The library does not point to a statute that defines it, so the wording of the recorded deed controls what it does.

Can I sell my house after signing a lady bird deed?

Yes. The State Law Library says the owner can live on the property, sell it, and change or revoke the deed. Expect the buyer's closing agent to read the recorded deed and ask about any mortgage.

Does a lady bird deed avoid probate in Texas?

It can move the house to the named beneficiary outside probate, according to the State Law Library. The beneficiary should still record the paperwork the county clerk requires.

Is there an official Texas form for a lady bird deed?

No. The library says no official form exists, and it points to sample language in legal publications. Have a lawyer draft or check the deed.

What is the difference between a lady bird deed and a TODD?

A TODD is created under Chapter 114 of the Estates Code and allows backup beneficiaries. A lady bird deed rests on common law and cannot name alternates, and it may trigger a mortgage due-on-sale clause.

Squatters or a Title Dispute on Your Texas Property? Get a Cash Offer

Dealing with an unauthorized occupant or an inherited house with unclear possession? We buy houses as-is. Tell us about the property.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has two different things people call squatters rights: adverse possession, a claim to ownership that takes years, and a 2025 sheriff removal process for people who unlawfully entered a home. Adverse possession is in Civil Practice and Remedies Code Chapter 16. The removal process is Property Code Chapter 24B, effective September 1, 2025. This guide explains both from the statutes.

What is adverse possession in Texas?

The statute defines adverse possession as an actual and visible appropriation of real property, started and continued under a claim of right that is inconsistent with and hostile to another person's claim (CPRC Sec. 16.021). The owner's right to sue to recover the property expires after a set number of years, and then the possessor has full title (Sec. 16.030).

A person cannot acquire by adverse possession any right to land dedicated to public use (Sec. 16.030).

How many years does it take?

Texas has several limitation periods, and which one applies depends on the facts:

  • 3 years: possession under title or color of title (Sec. 16.024).
  • 5 years: the possessor cultivates, uses or enjoys the property, pays taxes and claims under a duly registered deed. This does not apply to claims based on a quitclaim deed, a forged deed or a deed under a forged power of attorney (Sec. 16.025).
  • 10 years: the possessor cultivates, uses or enjoys the property. Without a title instrument, possession is limited to 160 acres unless the enclosed land is larger (Sec. 16.026).
  • 25 years: applies even if the owner had a legal disability, and also covers a good-faith possessor under a recorded deed (Secs. 16.027 and 16.028).

Time does not run while the owner is under 18, of unsound mind or serving in the armed forces in time of war, except for the 25-year limits (Sec. 16.022). Texas cases add more detail on hostility and exclusivity, and we did not review court decisions, so talk to an attorney about a specific claim.

Adverse possession between heirs

Heirs who inherit undivided interests can sometimes acquire the other heirs' shares. Sec. 16.0265 requires 10 continuous years of exclusive possession, payment of all taxes, an affidavit of heirship and an affidavit of adverse possession filed in the county deed records, four consecutive weeks of newspaper publication and certified-mail notice to the other heirs. A cotenant heir must file a controverting affidavit or sue within 5 years after the affidavits are filed.

If you share a family house with relatives who do not live there, this matters to both sides. See our guide to the Texas affidavit of heirship.

Removing a squatter under Chapter 24B

Chapter 24B lets the owner of residential real property, or the owner's agent, ask the county sheriff or constable to immediately remove a person who unlawfully entered and occupies a dwelling without consent. It applies only if all of these are true (Sec. 24B.001):

  • The property was not open to the public when the person entered, and no litigation is pending between the owner and the person.
  • The owner or agent told the person to leave and they did not.
  • The person is not a current or former tenant under an oral or written lease and is not an immediate family member of the owner.

The owner submits a complaint in the statutory form to the sheriff or constable of the county where the property is located, with government-issued ID (Sec. 24B.002). The form states that the person is not a tenant, that any lease the person produces is fraudulent and that any title naming the person as owner is fraudulent. The officer verifies the complainant is the record owner or agent, serves notice to vacate by hand or posting without delay and puts the owner in possession (Sec. 24B.003). The officer may charge a fee equal to a writ-of-possession fee.

A person who is wrongfully removed can sue the requester for actual damages, exemplary damages equal to three times the fair market rent, court costs and attorney's fees (Sec. 24B.005). The chapter does not limit other remedies or an officer's authority to arrest for trespass, vandalism or theft (Sec. 24B.006).

When someone is a tenant, not a squatter

If the occupant ever had a lease, Chapter 24B does not apply, and you use the eviction process instead. Our guide to the Texas eviction process covers the notice, justice court and writ steps. We could not confirm from an official page how sheriffs handle Chapter 24B requests in practice, including fees and forms, so ask your county sheriff or constable's office.

Texas squatters rights FAQ

How long does adverse possession take in Texas?

Between 3 and 25 years depending on the facts: 3, 5, 10 or 25 years under Civil Practice and Remedies Code Secs. 16.024 to 16.028.

Can a squatter claim my house in Texas?

Only after meeting the statutory possession period and showing actual, visible possession hostile to the owner's claim (Sec. 16.021). Paying taxes and holding a recorded deed shorten the period in some cases.

How do I remove a squatter in Texas?

If the person unlawfully entered, was never a tenant and is not an immediate family member, you can submit a Chapter 24B complaint to the county sheriff or constable (Property Code Secs. 24B.001 to 24B.003). Otherwise use the eviction process.

What if I remove someone who was really a tenant?

The person can sue for actual damages, three times the fair market rent in exemplary damages, costs and attorney's fees (Sec. 24B.005).

A Texas eviction starts with a written notice to vacate, then a sworn petition in the justice court of the precinct where the property sits, and it ends with a writ of possession executed by an officer. The rules are in Property Code Chapter 24 and the Texas Rules of Civil Procedure. This guide walks through the statutory steps landlords follow and what each deadline is.

Step 1: the notice to vacate

A tenant under a written lease or an oral rental agreement who defaults or holds over must get at least 3 days' written notice to vacate before the landlord files a forcible detainer suit, unless the lease sets a shorter or longer period (Property Code Sec. 24.005(a)). If the tenancy ends only for nonpayment and the tenant was not previously late, the notice must be a notice to pay rent or vacate.

The notice can be sent by mail (first class, registered, certified or by a delivery service), left inside the premises in a conspicuous place, hand delivered to any tenant 16 or older or, if the parties agreed in writing, sent by email or other electronic means (Sec. 24.005(f-3)). If a person entered by forcible entry, the owner gives oral or written notice to vacate before filing (Sec. 24.005(d)).

When a buyer at a tax or trustee foreclosure sale takes a building with a residential tenant who pays on time and is not in default, the buyer must give at least 30 days' written notice to vacate if it does not continue the lease (Sec. 24.005(b)).

Step 2: file in justice court

An eviction suit is filed in the justice court of the precinct where the property is located (Sec. 24.004). The petition must be sworn (Sec. 24.00505). Counterclaims and joinder of third parties are not allowed, and the justice court cannot decide title to the property (Sec. 24.0041). Courts cannot add local petition requirements or order pretrial mediation (Sec. 24.00506).

The Texas Supreme Court amended Rule 510 of the Rules of Civil Procedure, which governs eviction cases, with an effective date of January 1, 2026. We read only the court's preliminary-approval order, so check the current text of Rule 510 on txcourts.gov for petition contents and joinder of unpaid rent.

Step 3: service and trial

  • The sheriff or constable must make a diligent effort to serve the citation by the 5th business day after filing. If it is not served, the landlord can use another trained officer (Sec. 24.0051(f)).
  • Trial is held not earlier than the 10th day or later than the 21st day after filing, and not earlier than the 4th day after service. It cannot be postponed more than 7 days unless the parties agree in writing (Sec. 24.0051(g)).
  • A landlord can file a sworn motion for summary disposition. The tenant can defeat it by filing a response with supporting facts by the 4th day after service (Sec. 24.005106).
  • In justice court, parties can appear themselves or through an authorized agent who need not be an attorney (Sec. 24.011).

Chapter 24 counts weekends and holidays, but a deadline that lands on one moves to the next day that is not (Sec. 24.0042).

Step 4: judgment and writ of possession

A prevailing landlord gets a judgment for possession and a writ of possession. The writ cannot issue before the 6th day after judgment unless a possession bond is filed and approved (Sec. 24.0061). The officer posts a warning on the front door saying the writ will be executed not sooner than 24 hours later. The officer can use reasonable force, and the tenant's belongings are placed outside the unit.

Either side can appeal by filing a bond, a cash deposit or a statement of inability to pay costs by the 5th day after the judgment is signed (Sec. 24.005107). In a residential appeal the tenant must pay rent into the court registry, with the first payment due within 5 days of filing, or risk a writ without a hearing (Sec. 24.0053).

Attorney's fees

To recover attorney's fees, the landlord must send a written demand to vacate by registered or certified mail at least 10 days before suit. It must say fees can be recovered if the tenant does not vacate before the 11th day after receipt, unless a written lease already provides for fees (Sec. 24.006).

Texas eviction FAQ

How long is the notice to vacate in Texas?

At least 3 days in writing unless the lease sets a different period (Property Code Sec. 24.005(a)).

Where do I file an eviction in Texas?

In the justice court of the precinct where the property is located (Sec. 24.004).

How long does a Texas eviction take?

Trial is set between the 10th and 21st day after filing, and a writ cannot issue before the 6th day after judgment (Secs. 24.0051 and 24.0061). Appeals add time.

Can I evict a tenant without a court order?

No. Only an officer executing a writ of possession can remove a tenant after judgment (Sec. 24.0061).

A Texas affidavit of heirship is a sworn statement of a decedent's family history that is recorded in the county deed records, and under Estates Code Sec. 203.001 a court treats it as prima facie evidence of the facts once it has been of record for five years. The statute does not say that the affidavit by itself transfers title, and we did not find an official page that says so. Read this guide before relying on one to sell a house.

What the statute says it is

Under Sec. 203.001, a court in a heirship proceeding or a suit involving title must receive a statement of facts about family history, genealogy, marital status or the identity of heirs as prima facie evidence if two things are true. The statement is in an affidavit or instrument legally executed and acknowledged or sworn before an officer authorized to take oaths, or in a court judgment. And the affidavit has been of record for five years or more in the deed records.

The five years can run in the deed records of a county where the property is located when the title suit begins, or the county where the decedent lived at death. If a recorded affidavit contains an error, anyone interested in the proceeding can prove the true facts. It does not affect the rights of an omitted heir or a creditor of the decedent (Sec. 203.001).

The suggested form

Sec. 203.002 gives language that an affidavit may follow in substantially this form. It covers what the affiant knows, the decedent's date of death and residence, marital history, children, parents and siblings if there are no descendants, whether there was a will or administration, debts, unpaid estate or inheritance taxes, real property owned and the heirs.

The affiant should be someone with personal knowledge of the family. The affidavit is signed before a notary or other authorized officer and then recorded with the county clerk where the property is located or where the decedent was domiciled.

Where it is used

  • As evidence in a suit about title or a proceeding to declare heirship, once of record five years (Sec. 203.001).
  • As one of the filings an heir needs to claim co-heirs' shares by adverse possession (CPRC Sec. 16.0265). See Texas squatters rights and adverse possession.
  • As a comparison point for a small estate affidavit. That affidavit can transfer a decedent's homestead when it is the only real property in the estate, and a buyer who relies on it without notice of an undisclosed heir takes free of that heir's interest, subject to creditor claims (Estates Code Sec. 205.006).

What we could not confirm

We did not confirm whether title companies or lenders accept an affidavit of heirship for a sale before it has been of record five years. The statute addresses weight as evidence in court, not closing practice. We also did not open the statute on judicial declarations of heirship in Chapter 202, county recording fees or e-recording rules. If you plan to sell, ask your title company early what it needs, since it will decide what documents it requires.

Other ways inherited property moves

Depending on whether there was a will, an inherited house may move through a muniment of title, a small estate affidavit, probate or intestate succession.

Texas affidavit of heirship FAQ

What is an affidavit of heirship in Texas?

A sworn statement of a decedent's family history that is recorded in the deed records. Estates Code Sec. 203.001 makes it prima facie evidence in court after it has been of record five years.

Does an affidavit of heirship transfer title?

The statute we reviewed does not say that it does. It addresses evidence in court (Sec. 203.001).

Where is it recorded?

In the deed records of the county where the property is located or where the decedent was domiciled (Sec. 203.001).

Can an omitted heir still claim?

Yes. The statute says the affidavit does not affect the rights of an omitted heir or a creditor (Sec. 203.001).

Who can use a small estate affidavit?

Sec. 205.001 lets the distributees of an intestate decedent take the estate without waiting for a personal representative if the estate assets, not counting the homestead and exempt property, exceed known liabilities, and all of these are true:

  • The decedent died intestate and 30 days have passed since the death.
  • No petition for appointment of a personal representative is pending or has been granted.
  • The value of estate assets on the date of the affidavit, excluding homestead and exempt property, does not exceed $75,000.
  • The affidavit is filed with the clerk of the court that has jurisdiction and venue of the estate, and the judge approves it (Secs. 205.001 and 205.003).

Who signs and what it must say

Two disinterested witnesses and each distributee with legal capacity swear to the affidavit. For a minor or incapacitated distributee, a guardian or next of kin signs where warranted (Sec. 205.002). The affidavit lists all known assets and liabilities, marking assets claimed as exempt, the name and address of each distributee and family history facts showing each person's right to receive property.

Distributees give a copy of the affidavit, certified by the court clerk, to each person who owes money to the estate, holds estate property or acts as registrar, fiduciary or transfer agent for estate property (Sec. 205.004).

A buyer who relies on it without notice of an undisclosed heir takes free of that heir's interest, subject to creditor claims. Otherwise Chapter 205 does not transfer title to real property (Sec. 205.008).

Liability for the people who sign

Anyone who signs the affidavit is liable for damage or loss from payments or transfers made in reliance on it, and distributees must account to a personal representative appointed later (Sec. 205.007). $75,000 in estate assets on the date of the affidavit, not counting the homestead and exempt property (Estates Code Sec. 205.001).

The decedent must have died intestate and 30 days must have passed (Sec. 205.001).

Does the judge have to approve it?

Yes. The affidavit is filed with the court clerk and the judge approves it before it takes effect (Secs. 205.001 and 205.003).

Can a small estate affidavit transfer a house?

Only the decedent's homestead, and only if it is the only real property in the estate. It is then recorded in the county deed records (Sec. 205.006).

A Texas warranty deed conveys real estate with a covenant of general warranty, meaning the seller promises to defend the buyer's title against anyone lawfully claiming it. Property Code Sec. 5.022 gives a statutory form for it. Texas statutes do not use the names "general warranty deed" or "special warranty deed," so this guide sticks to what the code says.

What a conveyance has to be

A conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold or an estate for more than one year in land must be in writing, signed and delivered by the owner or an agent authorized in writing (Property Code Sec. 5.021). An estate is a fee simple unless express words or operation of law limit it (Sec. 5.001). A deed that purports to convey more than the grantor can lawfully convey passes only what the grantor owns (Sec. 5.003). An instrument that fails as a conveyance under Chapter 5 can still be enforced as a contract to convey, to the extent the law allows (Sec. 5.002).

The statutory warranty form

Sec. 5.022 provides a form, or one the same in substance, that conveys fee simple with a covenant of general warranty. It uses the words granted, sold and conveyed, states the consideration, describes the premises and includes a warranty to warrant and forever defend against every person lawfully claiming the premises. A warranty covenant is not required, and the parties may use any form or clause that does not violate the law (Sec. 5.022).

Using the words grant or convey in a conveyance of an estate of inheritance or fee simple implies two covenants unless the deed says otherwise: the grantor has not already conveyed the estate to someone else, and the estate is free from encumbrances at signing. Encumbrance includes a tax, an assessment and a lien. Either implied covenant can support a lawsuit as if it were written out (Secs. 5.023 and 5.024).

Signing and recording

A deed cannot be recorded unless the grantor signed and acknowledged or swore to it before an authorized officer, or signed before two or more credible subscribing witnesses. A person who presents it in person for recording must show photo ID to the county clerk (Sec. 12.001). A paper document needs an original acknowledged signature, or must be a certified copy of an electronic record (Sec. 12.0011).

You record with the county clerk of the county where the property is located. Fees and e-recording rules vary by county and we did not confirm them here.

Fixing a mistake in a recorded deed

A correction instrument can fix errors under Secs. 5.027 to 5.029. A nonmaterial or clerical correction can be made by a person with personal knowledge. A material correction must be signed by each party to the original instrument, or their heirs, successors or assigns, and recorded in each county where the original was recorded.

A deed term that bars sale, lease or transfer based on race, color, religion or national origin is void (Sec. 5.026).

What we could not confirm

A deed that conveys fee simple with a covenant of general warranty, as in the statutory form in Property Code Sec. 5.022.

Is a warranty covenant required in Texas?

No. A covenant of warranty is not required, and the parties can use any form that does not violate the law (Sec. 5.022).

What does the word convey imply?

Unless the deed says otherwise, the grantor has not previously conveyed the estate and it is free from encumbrances such as taxes and liens at signing (Secs. 5.023 and 5.024).

How do I fix an error in a recorded deed?

Record a correction instrument under Secs. 5.027 to 5.029. Material errors need signatures from each party to the original, or their heirs and successors.

A muniment of title is a Texas court order that admits a will to probate only to prove who owns the property, without opening a full estate administration. It is available when the estate owes no debt other than debt secured by a lien on real estate, or when the court finds some other reason administration is unnecessary. The rules are in Estates Code Chapter 257.

When a court will allow it

Under Sec. 257.001 a court may admit a will as a muniment of title if it is satisfied that the will should be admitted and that the estate owes no unpaid debt other than debt secured by a lien on real estate, or that administration is unnecessary for another reason. The applicant must prove that the testator died, that four years have not passed since the death, that the court has jurisdiction and venue, that citation was served and returned, that there is no unpaid debt of the kind described, and that the testator did not revoke the will (Sec. 257.054).

If the will is not self-proved, the applicant must also prove it was properly executed and that the testator was of sound mind and either 18 or older, married or had been married, or in the armed forces (Sec. 257.054).

What the application contains

The application includes the applicant's name and domicile, the last three numbers of the driver's license or Social Security number for the applicant and the testator, facts about the death and venue, a general description and probable value of the property, the date of the will, the executor's name and address, subscribing witnesses, after-born children, dissolved marriages and whether the state or a charity is a devisee (Sec. 257.051).

The will is filed with the application if the applicant controls it, and it stays in the county clerk's custody unless a court orders it removed (Sec. 257.052). If the will cannot be produced, the application states why, the contents as known and each devisee and heir with address and relationship (Sec. 257.053).

What the order does

An order admitting the will as a muniment of title is enough legal authority for anyone who owes the estate money, holds estate property or acts as registrar or transfer agent to pay or transfer the asset without administration, and without liability to the person described in the will (Sec. 257.102). A person entitled to property under the will can deal with it as if record title were in that person's name.

The court may also include a declaratory judgment construing the will on application and notice. Against an omitted person, that judgment is conclusive in a suit with a bona fide purchaser for value without actual notice (Sec. 257.101).

After the order

  • Within 180 days after the will is admitted, the applicant files a sworn affidavit with the court clerk saying which will terms have and have not been fulfilled. The court can waive or extend this, and failing to file does not affect title passing under the will (Sec. 257.103).
  • The order does not stop the court from later appointing a personal representative if an application is filed by the fourth anniversary of death, or if administration becomes necessary for a reason in Sec. 301.002(b) (Sec. 257.151).

When the estate owes no debt other than debt secured by a lien on real estate, or there is another reason administration is unnecessary (Sec. 257.001).

When a Texas resident dies without a will, Estates Code Chapter 201 decides who inherits, and the answer depends on whether there is a spouse, children, parents or siblings and on whether the property is community or separate. This guide summarizes the statute's main rules. It does not cover homestead rights, which Chapter 201 does not address.

If there is no surviving spouse

The estate passes to the children and their descendants. If there are none, it goes equally to the father and mother. If only one parent survives, half goes to that parent and half to siblings and their descendants, or all to the parent if there are no siblings or sibling descendants. If neither parent survives, it goes to siblings and their descendants (Sec. 201.001).

If none of those relatives survive, the estate splits into two moieties, one to paternal kindred and one to maternal kindred, passing through grandparents and their descendants (Sec. 201.001).

Separate property with a surviving spouse

  • Spouse and children or their descendants: the spouse takes one-third of the personal estate and a life estate in one-third of the land. The rest goes to the children or descendants, with the remainder in the land (Sec. 201.002).
  • Spouse and no child or descendant: the spouse takes all the personal estate and one-half of the land without remainder. The other half of the land passes by the rules in Sec. 201.001 (Sec. 201.002).
  • No surviving parent, sibling or their descendants: the spouse takes the entire estate (Sec. 201.002).

Community property

Community property passes to the surviving spouse if no child or descendant survives, or if all surviving children and descendants are also the surviving spouse's (Sec. 201.003). If the deceased spouse had a child or descendant who is not also the surviving spouse's, the deceased spouse's undivided one-half of the community passes to those children or descendants, charged with community debts.

Other rules that affect a sale

  • An adopted child inherits as a natural child, including a child who was equitably adopted (Sec. 201.054).
  • A person must be born before or in gestation at the death and survive by at least 120 hours (Sec. 201.056).
  • Descendants take per capita with representation, meaning each descendant of a deceased person takes that person's share (Sec. 201.101).
  • Heirs take as if the decedent were the original purchaser (Sec. 201.103).
  • A good-faith buyer for value from heirs who relies on an affidavit of heirship that omits a non-presumed child not yet adjudicated an heir gets good title to the interest the heirs would have had, and the heirs remain liable for the proceeds to the omitted child (Sec. 201.053).

Texas intestate succession FAQ

Who inherits if there is no will in Texas?

It depends on the family. With no spouse, children inherit first, then parents, then siblings and more distant kin (Estates Code Sec. 201.001). A spouse's share depends on whether the property is separate or community (Secs. 201.002 and 201.003).

What does a surviving spouse get in Texas?

From community property, the spouse takes it all if there are no children or all children are also the spouse's. From separate property, the share depends on whether children survive (Secs. 201.002 and 201.003).

Do adopted children inherit?

Yes, as natural children, including equitably adopted children (Sec. 201.054).

How long must an heir survive?

At least 120 hours after the death (Sec. 201.056).

In Texas a will does not prove title to property until it is admitted to probate (Estates Code Sec. 256.001), and it generally must be offered within four years of the testator's death. This guide covers what Chapter 256 says about the application, proof, the order and later challenges. We could not confirm typical timelines, filing fees or which court hears a given estate.

The four-year rule

A will may not be admitted to probate after the fourth anniversary of the testator's death unless the applicant proves that they were not in default in failing to present it by then (Sec. 256.003). Letters testamentary cannot issue on a will admitted after that date unless the application was filed on or before the fourth anniversary. A buyer for value in good faith, without knowledge of a will, who buys from heirs after the fourth anniversary has good title to the interest the heirs would have had, against a devisee under a later-offered will.

Who applies and what to file

An executor named in the will, a designated administrator, an independent administrator designated by all distributees or any interested person can apply to probate a will, even one that is lost, destroyed or from out of state. The application can be combined with one for appointment of an executor or administrator (Sec. 256.051).

It states details about the applicant and testator, the last three numbers of each person's driver's license or Social Security number, facts of death and venue, a description and probable value of property, the will date, the executor, witnesses, after-born children, dissolved marriages and any state or charity devisee, and that the executor is not disqualified (Sec. 256.052). The will is filed with the application and stays with the county clerk unless a court orders otherwise (Sec. 256.053).

What must be proved

The applicant proves the testator is dead, four years have not passed, the court has jurisdiction and venue, citation was served and returned, and the person seeking letters is entitled and not disqualified. The applicant also shows the will was not revoked and, if it is not self-proved, was validly executed (Secs. 256.151 and 256.152).

An unproved attested will can be proved by the sworn testimony or affidavit of one or more subscribing witnesses. A holographic will that is not self-proved can be proved by two witnesses to the testator's handwriting (Secs. 256.153 and 256.154).

The order and what follows

  • After the hearing the court enters an order admitting the will, and certified copies can be recorded in other counties (Sec. 256.201). The original will and the probate are deposited with the county clerk where probated (Sec. 256.202).
  • An interested person can contest the will's validity within two years after it is admitted. For forgery or fraud the two years run from discovery, and an incapacitated person has two years after the disability ends (Sec. 256.204).
  • A lawful will found after letters of administration were granted can still be proved. The court revokes the earlier letters, and the first administrator's acts remain as valid as if no will had been found (Sec. 256.103).

If the estate owes no debt other than a mortgage, a muniment of title can be simpler. With no will, see intestate succession.

What we could not confirm

No official page we opened states how long probate typically takes, the citation and hearing waiting periods, filing fees, or which court (county, constitutional county or statutory probate) hears an estate in your county. We also did not review independent and dependent administration, inventory or creditor deadlines in later chapters. Ask the clerk of your county court or an attorney.

Texas probate FAQ

How long do I have to probate a will in Texas?

Generally within four years of the testator's death, unless the applicant proves they were not in default (Estates Code Sec. 256.003).

Does a will prove title without probate?

No. A will is not effective to prove title or right to possession until admitted to probate, with an exception for foreign wills (Sec. 256.001).

Who can apply to probate a will?

An executor named in the will, a designated administrator, an independent administrator designated by all distributees or any interested person (Sec. 256.051).

How long can the will be contested?

Two years after it is admitted. Forgery or fraud claims run two years from discovery (Sec. 256.204).

In Texas, neither spouse can sell, convey or encumber the homestead without the other spouse's signature, whether the homestead is separate or community property. That rule is in Family Code Sec. 5.001. The code also sets who manages community and separate property and has a court process for selling when a spouse has disappeared or abandoned the home.

Separate and community property

Separate property is what a spouse owned before marriage, received during marriage by gift, devise or descent, and personal injury recoveries other than loss of earning capacity (Family Code Sec. 3.001). Community property is anything else acquired by either spouse during marriage (Sec. 3.002). Property held by either spouse during or at the end of marriage is presumed community, and proving otherwise takes clear and convincing evidence (Sec. 3.003).

Who manages what

  • Each spouse has sole management and control of that spouse's separate property (Sec. 3.101).
  • Each spouse has sole management of the community property they would have owned if single, such as personal earnings, revenue from separate property and personal injury recoveries (Sec. 3.102).
  • Mixed community property and community property not under sole management is under joint management unless the spouses agree otherwise by written power of attorney or other agreement (Sec. 3.102).
  • Property held in one spouse's name is presumed to be under that spouse's sole management, and a third person without fraud and without notice can rely on that authority (Sec. 3.104).

We did not open the definition of homestead or how title companies document joinder, so ask your title company what it will need.

If a court has declared one spouse incapacitated, the competent spouse of a community homestead, or the owner of a separate-property homestead, can sell without the other spouse's joinder (Secs. 5.002 and 5.003).

If a spouse is missing or has abandoned the home

A spouse can file a sworn petition to sell a homestead without the other spouse's joinder if the other spouse has disappeared, has permanently abandoned the homestead or is reported as a prisoner of war or missing on public service (Secs. 5.101 and 5.102). The petition goes to a court in the county where any part of the property is located, no earlier than the 60th day after the event, or six months after a POW or missing report (Sec. 5.103).

The court can appoint an attorney for the other spouse, and must for a POW or missing spouse. After notice and a hearing it issues an order it considers just and equitable, can add conditions or require a bond and can direct sale proceeds to the court registry (Secs. 5.104 and 5.106).

Recording

A schedule of separate real property is not constructive notice to a good-faith purchaser or creditor unless acknowledged and recorded in the deed records of the county where the property is located (Sec. 3.004). The same goes for a Subchapter D order affecting real property (Sec. 3.308). We did not review how divorce affects a sale or what happens when only one spouse is on the deed.

Texas community property home sale FAQ

Can one spouse sell the family home in Texas?

Not the homestead. Neither spouse can sell, convey or encumber it without the other spouse's joinder, with limited exceptions (Family Code Sec. 5.001).

What if my spouse abandoned the home?

A spouse can file a sworn petition to sell without joinder if the other spouse disappeared or permanently abandoned the homestead (Secs. 5.101 and 5.102).

Is property bought during marriage community property?

Generally yes, if acquired by either spouse during marriage and not separate property (Secs. 3.002 and 3.003).

Does a separate property home still need both signatures?

If it is the homestead, yes (Sec. 5.001).

In Texas, a mortgage is usually secured by a deed of trust, and if you default, the lender can sell the house at a public auction on the first Tuesday of a month without going to court. The sale rules are in Property Code Sec. 51.002. Notice of sale is due at least 21 days before the sale, and a residential borrower in default gets a separate notice with at least 20 days to cure.

What a deed of trust is

The code defines a security instrument as a deed of trust, mortgage or other contract lien on an interest in real property. The borrower who grants the lien is the mortgagor, and the lender or holder is the mortgagee (Property Code Sec. 51.0001). A trustee named in the instrument has the power of sale. The trustee's only duty is to exercise that power under the instrument's terms, and the trustee is not a fiduciary of the borrower or lender (Sec. 51.0074). A substitute trustee can be appointed by the mortgagee or servicer (Sec. 51.0075).

The foreclosure sale rules

  • Sale is a public auction between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of a month. If that Tuesday is January 1 or July 4, it moves to the first Wednesday (Sec. 51.002).
  • It is held at the county courthouse where the land is located, in the area the commissioners court designated, or if none, the area named in the notice of sale (Sec. 51.002).
  • It must begin at the time in the notice or within three hours after (Sec. 51.002).
  • The buyer takes the property as is, without warranties except warranties of title (Sec. 51.009).

Notices the borrower should get

For residential property, the servicer must first send a certified-mail notice of default that gives at least 20 days to cure (Sec. 51.002). Only after that can the notice of sale go out. The notice of sale must be given at least 21 days before the sale by posting at the courthouse door, filing a copy with the county clerk and serving written notice by certified mail on each debtor obligated to pay the debt. Service is complete when the notice is mailed to the last known address, so a borrower must tell the servicer about any change of address (Secs. 51.002 and 51.0021).

The notice must state the sender's name and address and include a conspicuous military-service statement (Sec. 51.002).

The sale date is on the notice, so you can plan around it. A sale before that date can pay the loan off from the proceeds, which can protect your credit and any equity you have. Read our guide to the Texas foreclosure process for more.

Does Texas require court for foreclosure?

A sale under a power of sale in a deed of trust is a public auction held under Property Code Sec. 51.002, without a court case. Other ways exist, which we did not cover.

When are Texas foreclosure sales held?

The first Tuesday of the month between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., or the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4 (Sec. 51.002).

How much notice do I get?

At least 21 days for the notice of sale and, for residential property in default, a prior notice giving at least 20 days to cure (Sec. 51.002).

Does the buyer get a warranty?

Only warranties of title. The property is sold as is (Sec. 51.009).

A Texas lender that uses the power of sale in a deed of trust must send a default notice with at least 20 days to cure on a home loan, then give at least 21 days' notice of sale, and the auction takes place on the first Tuesday of a month. This guide explains those notices, your options before the sale and what Property Code Chapter 51 says about deeds in lieu, deficiency claims and rescission.

The timeline

For residential property, the servicer first serves a certified-mail notice of default that gives at least 20 days to cure. If you do not cure, the notice of sale follows. It must be given at least 21 days before the sale by posting at the courthouse door, filing with the county clerk and certified mail to each debtor (Property Code Sec. 51.002). The sale is a public auction between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of the month at the county courthouse. See Texas deed of trust and foreclosure sale rules for the details.

Options before the sale

  • Contact your lender or servicer as soon as you know you will fall behind. The Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs says alternatives to foreclosure exist if you have fallen behind.
  • HUD-approved foreclosure counseling is free. The TDHCA page lists 1-800-569-4287 and the Homeowner's HOPE Hotline at 1-888-995-HOPE (4673). We did not confirm which federal programs on that page are still active.
  • If the problem is delinquent property tax, a debtor is not in default under a residential deed of trust for that reason if the debtor gave the servicer notice at least 10 days before entering a tax installment agreement under Tax Code Sec. 33.02 and the property is protected from seizure under that law (Property Code Sec. 51.0011).
  • Sell the house before the sale date. A closing before the sale can pay off the loan from the proceeds, and any equity left is yours.

Deed in lieu of foreclosure

A deed in lieu transfers the house to the lender instead of going through a sale. If you did not disclose a lien or encumbrance and the holder had no personal knowledge of it, the holder can void the deed before the fourth anniversary of its execution and foreclose under the original deed of trust. A holder that accepts a deed in lieu can still foreclose without electing to void the deed, and its priority is not affected (Sec. 51.006).

After the sale

  • Any action to recover a deficiency after a nonjudicial foreclosure must be brought within two years of the sale. A defendant can ask the court to find the fair market value at the sale date and get an offset if it exceeds the sale price (Sec. 51.003).
  • For residential property of one to four units or a condominium or cooperative unit, the mortgagee, trustee or substitute trustee can rescind the sale within 15 calendar days on listed grounds, such as unmet statutory requirements, a cure before the sale, a written cure agreement or a bankruptcy stay (Sec. 51.016).
  • A dwelling owned by a servicemember with a pre-service obligation cannot be sold during active duty or the nine months after, unless under a court order or a compliant waiver. Violation is a Class A misdemeanor, and a court can stay proceedings on application (Sec. 51.015).

Texas foreclosure FAQ

How long does foreclosure take in Texas?

The statute requires at least 20 days to cure on a residential default notice and at least 21 days' notice of sale (Property Code Sec. 51.002). Real timelines depend on the lender.

When are Texas foreclosure auctions?

The first Tuesday of the month between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. at the county courthouse, or the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4 (Sec. 51.002).

Can the lender sue for a deficiency?

Within two years of the sale, and the borrower can ask the court to credit fair market value if it exceeds the sale price (Sec. 51.003).

Can I sell my house before foreclosure?

Yes. A sale that closes before the auction can pay off the loan from the proceeds.

What the CFPB says

The CFPB says that when you buy a home you generally pay all the costs of the transaction, but depending on the contract or state law the seller may end up paying some of them. Common closing charges include appraisal fees, tax service provider fees, title insurance, government taxes and prepaid expenses such as property taxes, homeowners insurance and interest until the first payment. The Texas Real Estate Commission's One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026, leaves the option period length as a blank for the parties to fill in. Which TREC form applies

TREC lists Form 20-19 as its most frequently used contract, for the resale of a single family home, duplex, triplex or fourplex. It is not for condominiums, new homes sold by a builder or farm and ranch property. TREC's other forms include the Residential Condominium Contract (Resale) 30-18, the New Home Contracts 23-20 and 24-20, the Farm and Ranch Contract 25-17, the Unimproved Property Contract 9-18 and the Amendment to Contract 39-11. The form says it is intended only for trained real estate license holders and is not meant for complex transactions. It replaces Form 20-18.

The option period

  • The seller grants the buyer the unrestricted right to terminate by notice within a blank number of days after the effective date (paragraph 5B). Notice must be given by 5:00 p.m. local time where the property is located.
  • If the buyer terminates in the option period, the option fee goes to the seller and the earnest money is refunded to the buyer (5B).
  • The option fee and earnest money amounts are blanks. The buyer delivers them to the escrow agent within 3 days after the effective date, and the option fee is credited to the sales price at closing (5A).
  • If no option fee amount is stated or it is not delivered on time, the buyer has no unrestricted termination right under paragraph 5 (5D).

What is the option period in a Texas contract?

For Sale By Owner in Texas: Required Disclosures and What to Know

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • For Sale By Owner in Texas: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a For Sale By Owner in Texas sale
  • Turn the For Sale By Owner in Texas offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling Your Texas House Yourself? Get a Cash Offer First

No agent, no showings, no repairs. Compare a written cash offer with selling on your own.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Texas owner selling a home without an agent still has to give the buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice, and if the house will still be encumbered by a recorded lien at closing the seller must give a separate lien disclosure at least seven days before. Those duties are in Property Code Secs. 5.008 and 5.016. We could not confirm from TREC whether an owner needs a license to sell their own home.

The Seller's Disclosure Notice

A seller of residential real property with not more than one dwelling unit must give the buyer a written notice substantially like the statutory notice (Property Code Sec. 5.008). It covers the seller's knowledge as of the date signed, such as appliances, roof, defects, flooding history, floodplain, termites and lead-based paint. It is not a substitute for inspections or warranties. If something is unknown, the seller says so on the notice and complies (Sec. 5.008(d)).

The seller or agent has no duty to disclose a death by natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to property condition, or that a former occupant had HIV-related illness (Sec. 5.008(c)). Deliver the notice on or before the effective date of a binding contract. If you do not, the buyer can terminate within seven days after receiving it (Sec. 5.008(f)).

The notice does not apply to many transfers, including court-ordered or foreclosure sales, sales by fiduciaries of an estate or trust, transfers between co-owners, to a spouse or lineal relatives, to or from a governmental entity and never-occupied new homes (Sec. 5.008(e)). TREC publishes the form as 55-1.

Other federal and TREC notices

TREC also publishes a Notice to Prospective Buyer (58-0), a Seller's Disclosure about Groundwater and Surface Water Rights (61-0) and the federal lead-based paint addendum (56-0). Paragraph 7C of Form 20-19 says a lead-based paint disclosure is required by federal law for a dwelling built before 1978.

Compare with a cash offer?
No agent, no showings and no repairs. We buy as-is and you choose the closing date.
Get My Cash Offer →

The lien disclosure

Sec. 5.016 says a person cannot convey, or contract to convey, residential property that will be encumbered by a recorded lien at conveyance unless a separate written disclosure of at least 12-point type is given to the buyer and each lienholder on or before the seventh day before the earlier of conveyance or signing a binding contract or option. It must identify the property and each lienholder, state the debt and loan terms, say whether the lienholder consented, cover insurance and property taxes due, and start with the prescribed all-caps warning about possible demand for full payment.

A violation does not invalidate the conveyance, but the buyer can terminate on or before the seventh day after receiving the notice. The section has exceptions, including transfers where the buyer gets a title insurance policy insuring the transfer, and a violation is not actionable if the person reasonably believes, and acts to ensure, that each unnotified lien will be released within 30 days after title transfers (Sec. 5.016).

Do you need a license to sell your own home?

The Occupations Code defines a broker as a person who, in exchange for or expecting a commission or other valuable consideration, performs acts such as selling, listing or negotiating real estate for another person (Sec. 1101.002). The list of persons the chapter does not cover does not have a separate entry for a homeowner selling their own home (Sec. 1101.005). The TREC FAQ page we opened did not answer the question, so we state no TREC position. The definition applies to acts for another person.

Form 20-19 itself says it is intended for use by trained real estate license holders. See TREC Form 20-19 and the option period and Texas closing costs.

For sale by owner Texas FAQ

What disclosures does a Texas FSBO seller owe?

The Seller's Disclosure Notice under Property Code Sec. 5.008 for residential property with not more than one dwelling unit, and a separate lien disclosure under Sec. 5.016 if a recorded lien will encumber the property at closing.

What if I do not give the disclosure on time?

The buyer can terminate within seven days after receiving the Seller's Disclosure Notice (Sec. 5.008(f)) or the lien disclosure (Sec. 5.016(b)).

Do I have to disclose a death in the house?

The statute says there is no duty to disclose a death by natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to property condition (Sec. 5.008(c)).

Do I need a license to sell my own home?

We could not confirm a TREC position. The broker definition covers acts performed for another person (Occupations Code Sec. 1101.002).

What paperwork does a Texas owner need to sell a house without an agent?

A Texas owner selling without an agent still has to hand the buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice, use a written contract, and record a signed and acknowledged deed with the county clerk. No agent is needed for any of those steps, but each has rules attached.

The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) publishes the disclosure as Form 55-1, with an effective date of May 28, 2026. TREC describes it as required of sellers of previously occupied single family residences and as meant for contracts entered into on or after September 1, 2023. The notice carries the information that Section 5.008 of the Property Code calls for about material facts and the physical condition of the property.

  • Seller's Disclosure Notice (TREC 55-1) for a previously occupied single-family home
  • A federal lead-based paint disclosure if the house was built before 1978
  • A groundwater and surface water rights disclosure when the contract calls for it
  • Notice to Prospective Buyer (TREC 58-0), which covers title advice and utility district notices
  • A deed that is signed and acknowledged, then recorded in the land's home county

The TREC form page carries the current version. Sellers who are unsure which exemptions apply to their sale should ask a Texas real estate attorney, since the Property Code lists situations where the notice is not required.

Which disclosures apply, and where does each come from?

Some disclosures come from state law, some from the standard TREC contract, and one comes from federal law, so the list depends on the house and the contract.

Common disclosures for a Texas for-sale-by-owner house, with the agency that publishes each
DisclosureWhen it appliesPublished by
Seller's Disclosure Notice, Form 55-1Previously occupied single family residence, under Property Code Sec. 5.008TREC
Seller's Disclosure About Groundwater and Surface Water RightsDefault under TREC contracts unless every statement in Paragraph 7I(3) is trueTREC
Notice to Prospective Buyer, Form 58-0Abstract or title policy advice, and utility district noticesTREC
Lead-based paint disclosure and pamphletMost housing built before 1978U.S. EPA

The water disclosure is the one that surprises sellers. TREC says it is not required by any other law, so it arises only when the parties use a TREC contract, and the exemption from the Seller's Disclosure Notice does not automatically excuse it. A well, pond, lake or water tank on the lot, or any known severed or leased groundwater right, can make the form necessary.

TREC defines surface water rights as a permit, certified filing or certificate of adjudication from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality that allows diversion, impoundment or use of surface water. If you do not know whether your tract has one, ask an attorney.

What does federal law require for a house built before 1978?

The EPA's Lead-based Paint Disclosure Rule applies to most private housing built before 1978, and it puts the burden on the seller whether or not an agent is involved. The rule does not cover foreclosure sales, zero-bedroom units, housing built after 1977, or housing tested and found free of lead-based paint by a certified inspector.

  • Give the buyer the EPA pamphlet, Protect Your Family From Lead In Your Home.
  • Disclose what you know about lead-based paint and lead hazards, and hand over any records or reports.
  • Include a Lead Warning Statement in or attached to the contract, with confirmation that you complied.
  • Offer a 10-day window for a paint inspection or risk assessment, which the buyer may waive or the parties may change in writing.
  • Keep the signed disclosure for three years after the sale closes.

EPA publishes sample seller's disclosure forms in English and Spanish. A seller who fails to comply may face penalties, so an owner of an older Texas house should handle this before accepting an offer, not after.

Do I need a license to sell my own house in Texas?

TREC says a license is not required for an individual employed by a property owner to buy or sell real property on the owner's behalf, citing Rule 535.5(c). For a sale of your own house, confirm with TREC before relying on that answer.

That answer matters if title sits in an LLC or corporation and a family member or employee is handling the sale. It does not settle other situations, such as selling a property you do not own or taking a fee to market someone else's house. If the facts are unclear, a short call to a Texas real estate attorney costs less than a licensing complaint.

How do I record the deed and clear title in Texas?

A deed gets filed with the clerk of the county that holds the land, and it must be signed and acknowledged before an authorized officer such as a notary, or witnessed by two subscribing witnesses. The Texas county clerk manual lists general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's and sheriff's deeds among the instruments filed there.

Recording fees are set locally. Dallas, Denton and Ellis counties each print a $25 first-page charge on their fee schedules, and each charges $4 for later pages, with differences in add-ons. Ask the county clerk for the current fee page and any rules on return addresses, ID and payment, since those vary by county.

  • Title search. A title company or lawyer checks recorded liens, judgments and the chain of owners before closing.
  • Payoff and release. A mortgage balance is paid at closing and the lender records a release of lien.
  • Inherited houses. The State Law Library says no law forces third parties to accept an affidavit of heirship, and that a muniment of title, executor's deed or transfer on death deed may be needed instead.
  • Contracts for deed. Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D covers executory contracts for residential property, and the purchaser has a statutory right to cancel.

How do property taxes and exemptions factor into a Texas for-sale-by-owner sale?

The tax lien attaches on January 1 and the owner on that day is liable for the year, so the contract has to say who pays what for the year of sale. The Comptroller says appraisal districts value property as of January 1, tax bills go out around October 1, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on February 1 with a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

A buyer who takes title after January 1 can claim a homestead exemption for the rest of that year if the seller did not receive it. School districts must give a $140,000 residence homestead exemption, and owners 65 or older or disabled get an additional $60,000 school exemption. Sellers should bring tax receipts, exemption letters and any over-65 ceiling paperwork to the closing so the title company can prorate correctly.

Texas also sets a 10 percent annual cap on increases in appraised value for a residence homestead.

What if I am selling to stop a foreclosure?

A Texas homeowner facing non-judicial foreclosure has a short and fixed timeline, and selling before the auction is one way out. After a notice of default, the borrower may cure by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving it, and the servicer must send a Notice of Sale at least 21 days before the sale.

Foreclosure auctions are public and held between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of a month, or the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4, according to the Attorney General's informal guidance. A seller in this position should call the servicer, find out the sale date on the posted notice, and have a title company confirm the payoff before listing at a price the market will bear.

More questions about For Sale By Owner in Texas

Do I have to give a buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice if I sell my Texas house myself?

Generally yes. TREC describes Form 55-1 as required of sellers of previously occupied single family residences, based on Property Code Sec. 5.008. Having no agent does not remove the duty, though the statute lists situations where the notice does not apply.

Is the groundwater and surface water disclosure required by Texas law?

No. TREC says it is not required by another law. It becomes part of the deal when the parties use a TREC contract, unless every statement in Paragraph 7I(3) of the One to Four Family Residential Contract is true.

What is TREC Form 58-0?

It is the Notice to Prospective Buyer. TREC says it acknowledges that the buyer was advised to have an attorney examine the abstract or to buy a title insurance policy, and it carries statutory notices that matter if the property lies in a utility district.

Does a federal lead paint disclosure apply to my Texas home?

Only if the house was built before 1978. For most private housing from that era, the EPA rule requires the pamphlet, a disclosure of what you know, a Lead Warning Statement and a 10-day inspection window for the buyer.

Where do I record the deed after a for-sale-by-owner closing in Texas?

At the office of the clerk for the county that holds the house. The deed must be signed and acknowledged before a notary or other authorized officer, or witnessed by two subscribing witnesses, and the county sets its own fee and filing rules.

Owe Texas Property Taxes? Get a Cash Offer Before the Next Deadline

Unpaid property taxes can be paid from your sale proceeds at closing. Tell us about the house and get a written cash offer.
