Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has no state property tax. Local taxing units set rates, appraisal districts set values, and taxes are due by January 31 of the year after the tax year. Taxes for 2026 are due by January 31, 2027, which is a Sunday, so under Tax Code Sec. 1.06 the last day without penalty is Monday, February 1, 2027. This guide covers the vocabulary, the penalty schedule and what happens if taxes go unpaid. For county and city details, use our Texas county property tax guides.

Who does what

The Texas Comptroller says Texas has no state property tax and that its office does not collect property tax or set rates. Local taxing units do that. A county appraisal district sets the value of your property, each taxing unit adopts a rate, and one tax office usually sends the bill. Cities, counties, school districts and special districts can each tax the same house.

Rate vocabulary

After receiving the certified appraisal roll, most taxing units calculate two rates, according to the Comptroller's truth-in-taxation page:

  • No-new-revenue rate: a rate that would produce the same amount of tax if applied to the same properties taxed in both years.
  • Voter-approval rate: the maximum rate allowed by law without voter approval. For units other than school districts and special taxing units, it provides about the same revenue as the previous year for day-to-day operations plus an extra 3.5 percent, plus funds to pay debts. For special taxing units, the page says the extra is 8 percent.

If a unit adopts a rate above its voter-approval rate, the voters can force an election. Qualified voters can petition to require an election on cutting the adopted rate to the voter-approval rate, with signatures from at least three percent of registered voters (Tax Code Sec. 26.075). We did not confirm other rate-formula details from the statute.

Behind on property taxes?
Get My Cash Offer →

Penalty and interest

Delinquent tax carries penalty and interest that grow each month: 7 percent total in February, 9 percent in March, 11 percent in April, 13 percent in May, 15 percent in June and 18 percent in July (Sec. 33.01). Accounts still unpaid on July 1 can go to a delinquent tax attorney, who can add up to 20 percent (Sec. 33.07). Only the governing body of the taxing unit can waive penalty and interest, in situations listed in Sec. 33.011.

Liens and liability

A tax lien attaches to the property every January 1 (Sec. 32.01). The owner on that date is personally liable for that year's tax, and selling the house does not end the liability (Sec. 32.07). Taxing units can sue to foreclose the lien. See our guide to Texas tax deed sales and the property tax protest and homestead exemption guides for ways to lower the bill.

Paying in installments

Homeowners who are 65 or older or disabled can ask in writing to pay the homestead tax in four installments without penalty or interest (Sec. 31.031). A homeowner who pays a delinquent bill through a tax installment agreement under Sec. 33.02 can also affect whether the mortgage is in default for that reason. See the foreclosure guide.

Texas property tax FAQ

When are Texas property taxes due?

January 31 of the year after the tax year. Taxes for 2026 are due by January 31, 2027, which is a Sunday, so the last day to pay without penalty is Monday, February 1, 2027 (Tax Code Secs. 31.02 and 1.06).

What is the penalty for paying late?

7 percent in February, rising to 18 percent by July, plus up to 20 percent in attorney collection fees after June 30 (Secs. 33.01 and 33.07).

Does Texas have a state property tax?

No. The Comptroller says local taxing units set rates and collect the tax.

The Texas residence homestead exemption takes $140,000 off the value of your home for school district taxes, and homeowners who are 65 or older or disabled get an additional $60,000. The amounts are in Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) and (c) and Texas Constitution Article VIII Sec. 1-b. You apply through your county appraisal district.

What the exemption is worth

Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) gives an adult a $140,000 exemption from school district tax on the appraised value of the residence homestead, and Sec. 11.13(c) adds $60,000 for an adult who is disabled or 65 or older. The Comptroller's example: a $300,000 home with the $140,000 exemption pays school taxes as if it were worth $160,000. The Constitution has the same amounts in Art. VIII Sec. 1-b(c).

Other exemptions are local options. A taxing unit can adopt an exemption of a percentage of appraised value, not more than 20 percent and not less than $5,000 (Sec. 11.13(n)). Units can also adopt an additional exemption for those 65 or older or disabled, and the amount is $3,000 unless a larger amount is specified (Sec. 11.13(d) and (e)). Art. VIII Sec. 1-b also provides a $3,000 exemption for state purposes.

What counts as a residence homestead

  • The homestead includes land not exceeding 20 acres used in the residential occupancy of the structure (Sec. 11.13(j)).
  • It does not lose its character because of a temporary absence of less than two years with intent to return, military service, or residence in a facility providing health, infirmity or aging services (Sec. 11.13(l)).
  • Disabled means under a disability for purposes of federal disability insurance benefits (Sec. 11.13(m)).

Surviving spouses and the tax limit

A surviving spouse can keep the 65-or-older exemption from the same taxing unit if the deceased spouse died in a year in which they qualified, the survivor was 55 or older at the time and the property remains the survivor's homestead (Sec. 11.13(q)). For a homestead receiving the 65-or-older or disability exemption, school taxes may not increase while it remains that person's homestead, except to the extent of new improvements (Art. VIII Sec. 1-b(d)).

The appraisal cap

The appraisal office may raise a residence homestead's appraised value in a year to no more than the lesser of the most recent market value or the sum of 10 percent of last year's appraised value, last year's appraised value and the market value of new improvements (Sec. 23.23(a)). We did not review the later subsections of that section.

How to apply

The Comptroller lists the application as Form 50-114, filed with the appraisal district. We did not open the filing-deadline section, so confirm the deadline with your district. See also our guides on protesting your value and the Texas property tax guide. Disabled veteran and other exemptions exist, and we did not confirm their amounts.

Texas homestead exemption FAQ

How much is the Texas homestead exemption?

$140,000 for school district taxes, plus $60,000 more for homeowners who are 65 or older or disabled (Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) and (c)).

What is the homestead appraisal cap?

The appraised value of a residence homestead can rise by no more than 10 percent of last year's appraised value, plus new improvements, in a year (Sec. 23.23(a)).

Can a surviving spouse keep the exemption?

A surviving spouse who was 55 or older when the deceased spouse died can keep the 65-or-older exemption in some cases (Sec. 11.13(q)).

How many acres count as a homestead?

Up to 20 acres used in the residential occupancy of the structure (Sec. 11.13(j)).

To protest your Texas appraisal, file written notice with the appraisal review board by May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered to you, whichever is later. That rule is in Tax Code Sec. 41.44(a)(1). This guide follows the Comptroller's protest page and Tax Code Chapters 41 and 42 through the ARB hearing and appeals.

What you can protest

An owner can protest the appraised value, unequal appraisal, inclusion on the appraisal records, denial of a partial exemption and any other action that adversely affects the owner (Tax Code Sec. 41.41). The appraisal district sends a notice of appraised value by May 1, or April 1 for a residence homestead, or as soon as practical after, when the value is higher than the previous year (Sec. 25.19).

The deadline and the forms

The statute says written notice must be filed with the ARB not later than May 15 or the 30th day after the notice was delivered to the owner, whichever is later (Sec. 41.44(a)(1)). A late notice filed before the ARB approves the records gets a hearing if good cause is shown (Sec. 41.44(b)). The Comptroller's page words the 30 days as both delivery and mailing in different places, so rely on the statute's delivery language and file early.

Use Form 50-132, Property Owner's Notice of Protest. Use Form 50-162 to appoint an agent. A notice is sufficient if it identifies the property, the owner and a written statement of dissatisfaction with an appraisal district decision.

We buy as-is, pay taxes from the proceeds and charge no commission.

The ARB hearing

  • The ARB must send hearing notice at least 15 days in advance. At least 14 days before, the district must send the Taxpayer Assistance Pamphlet, the hearing procedures and a statement that you can request copies of the information it will use.
  • You can appear in person, by telephone or videoconference, or file a written affidavit.
  • ARB decisions bind only the tax year at issue. The Comptroller cannot advise on or intervene in a protest.

If you miss the deadline

The Comptroller lists late-protest options: a motion for correction if a homestead was appraised at least one-fourth above the correct value, or a non-homestead at least one-third above, and corrections for clerical errors that can reach the current year and five preceding tax years.

Appeals after the ARB

  • District court: file a petition for review within 60 days after receiving notice that a final order was entered, or the appeal is barred (Sec. 42.21). You must pay before the delinquency date the lesser of the taxes on the undisputed value, the taxes under the order or last year's taxes, or you forfeit the right to proceed (Sec. 42.08(b)).
  • SOAH: if the ARB value is over $1 million (not industrial property), file a notice with the chief appraiser within 30 days of the order and a $1,500 deposit within 90 days.
  • Regular binding arbitration: available if the property is a residence homestead of any value, or has appraised value of $5 million or less. The request goes to the Comptroller within 60 days of the order notice, with the required deposit.

We did not open Chapter 41A or the arbitration deposit amounts. See also our homestead exemption and property tax guides.

Texas property tax protest FAQ

When is the Texas protest deadline?

May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered to you, whichever is later (Tax Code Sec. 41.44(a)(1)).

Which form do I file?

Form 50-132, Property Owner's Notice of Protest, per the Comptroller.

How long do I have to appeal an ARB decision?

60 days after receiving notice of the final order to file a petition for review in district court (Sec. 42.21).

Do I have to pay taxes while I appeal?

You must pay before the delinquency date the lesser of the amounts in Sec. 42.08(b), usually the tax on the undisputed value.

Delinquent Taxes on Your Texas House? Get a Cash Offer Before a Sale

A cash sale can pay delinquent taxes before a tax sale. Tell us about the house and any sale date.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

After a Texas tax sale, a former owner of a homestead can redeem the property on or before the second anniversary of the purchaser's deed filing, but must pay a premium of 25 percent in the first year and 50 percent in the second. Other property has only 180 days, and the premium cannot exceed 25 percent. These rules come from Tax Code Chapter 34.

When and where tax sales happen

A sale (other than an online public auction) takes place between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of a month, or the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4 (Sec. 34.01(r-1)). Online public auctions can begin any time and must conclude at 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday (Sec. 34.01(r-2)). Sales occur at the county courthouse unless the commissioners court designates another nearby public place or online (Sec. 34.01(r)).

What the sale does

  • If no sufficient bid is received, the officer bids the property off to the taxing unit for the lesser of the judgment amount or market value, and the unit's title is subject only to the defendant's right of redemption (Sec. 34.01(j) and (k)).
  • A sale to someone other than a taxing unit extinguishes the liens for the taxes, penalties and interest in the judgment. It does not affect personal liability for amounts the proceeds did not cover (Sec. 34.01(q)).
  • Tax-sale deeds are filed with the county clerk (Sec. 34.01(m)).

Your right of redemption

Homestead or agricultural-use property sold to a buyer other than a taxing unit: redeem on or before the second anniversary of the date the purchaser's deed is filed for record. You pay the bid amount, the deed recording fee, taxes, penalties, interest and costs the purchaser paid, plus a premium of 25 percent of the total in year one or 50 percent in year two (Sec. 34.21(a)).

Other property: redeem not later than the 180th day after the deed is filed, with a premium that cannot exceed 25 percent (Sec. 34.21(e)). Homestead property bid off to a taxing unit has the two-year period too (Sec. 34.21(b) and (c)).

Redemption does not give the former owner use, possession or rents during the period, and the right cannot be transferred. Any instrument that purports to transfer it is void (Sec. 34.21(h) and (l)). You can request an itemization of costs, which the purchaser or collector must deliver within 10 days (Sec. 34.21(i)).

Resale, excess proceeds and challenges

  • A taxing unit that bought the property can resell it at any time by public or private sale, subject to redemption, and the redemption period starts when the deed to the unit is filed (Sec. 34.05). An action attacking the validity of a resale must be brought within one year (Sec. 34.05(f)).
  • The clerk holds excess sale proceeds for two years after the sale. A claim must be filed before the second anniversary. An attorney's fee to obtain excess proceeds cannot exceed the lesser of 25 percent or $1,000, and non-attorneys cannot charge a fee (Secs. 34.03 and 34.04).
  • To challenge a tax sale's validity, you must deposit the taxes, penalties, interest and costs into the court registry or file an affidavit of inability to pay (Sec. 34.08).

We did not open Chapter 33 on the judgment suits that come first, or county practices. Selling the house before the sale date can pay the taxes and protect your equity. See the Texas property tax guide.

Texas tax deed sales FAQ

How long do I have to redeem a homestead after a tax sale?

Until the second anniversary of the date the purchaser's deed is filed, with a 25 percent premium in year one and 50 percent in year two (Tax Code Sec. 34.21(a)).

How long for other property?

Not later than the 180th day after the deed is filed, with a premium of no more than 25 percent (Sec. 34.21(e)).

When are tax sales held?

The first Tuesday of the month between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., or the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4 (Sec. 34.01(r-1)).

Can I get money left over after a tax sale?

The clerk holds excess proceeds for two years, and a claim must be filed before the second anniversary of the sale (Sec. 34.03).

What TREC says about fees

TREC's consumer article on buying and selling a home says TREC does not regulate the fees paid to any real estate license holder, including buyer's agents, seller's agents, brokers, inspectors or appraisers, and that you should carefully review the fees in any representation or service agreement before you sign. TREC Form 20-19, paragraph 12B, says brokerage compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable, and lets a seller or buyer contribute at closing a dollar amount or percentage toward the other side's broker compensation.

Who gets paid

A TREC committee article about the then-pending National Association of Realtors settlement says TREC takes direction from the Legislature, which gave it narrow authority over license holder compensation, specifically that a broker is the one who gets paid. The same article describes ideas for a statement that fees to brokers are paid under separate agreements between parties and their brokers, or between brokers. The article is undated and described the settlement as not yet court-approved, so we do not state what changed afterward. We did not find a final TREC position on the settlement.

The Real Estate License Act, Occupations Code Chapter 1101, defines a broker as a person who acts in exchange for a commission or other valuable consideration, or expecting one. The intermediary provisions require that the parties' written consent state the source of any expected compensation to the broker.

The federal exclusion

According to IRS Publication 523 (2025), if you meet certain conditions you may exclude the first $250,000 of gain from the sale of your home from income, and the exclusion rises to $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly.

  • Ownership test: you owned the home at least 24 months out of the last five years before the sale date. For a married couple filing jointly, only one spouse has to meet it.

  • Depreciation: the exclusion is reduced to the extent of depreciation adjustments for rental or business use, and depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 is recognized.
  • Like-kind exchange: acquiring the home through a Section 1031 exchange is an automatic disqualification.

What the IRS page says

  • A like-kind exchange of real property used for business or held for investment, solely for like-kind business or investment property, generally results in no recognized gain or loss. If you also receive other property or money, gain is recognized to that extent, and a loss cannot be recognized.
  • After the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, Section 1031 applies only to exchanges of real property. Property held primarily for sale still does not qualify.

In Texas, the county clerk serves as the county recorder, and deeds and other instruments are recorded in the county where the property is located. Local Government Code Sec. 191.001 says so, citing Article V, Section 20 of the Texas Constitution. This guide covers what the statutes say about recording. Search portals and fees vary by county, and we did not confirm them for the state as a whole.

Where records live

The county clerk records an instrument in a well-bound book, except instruments kept on microfilm or another medium as provided in Chapters 204 and 205 (Local Government Code Sec. 191.002). Property Code Sec. 11.004 requires the clerk to correctly record, within a reasonable time, any instrument authorized or required to be recorded that is proved, acknowledged or sworn to, to give a receipt, to record instruments for the same property in the order filed and to keep the required indexes. Deeds from tax sales are also filed with the county clerk (Tax Code Sec. 34.01(m)).

Rules for what can be recorded

  • An instrument may not be recorded unless it is in English or complies with Property Code Sec. 11.002.
  • An instrument executed after December 31, 1981 conveying an interest in real property may not be recorded unless it shows a mailing address for each grantee, or a penalty filing fee equal to the greater of $25 or twice the statutory recording fee is paid (Sec. 11.003).
  • A deed must be acknowledged or sworn, and in-person filers must show photo ID. See Texas warranty deed for those rules.

Where do I search for records?
